qs.q: A 38-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill is scheduled to undergo an extensive open abdominal myomectomy. When should she stop her contraceptive medication?
o: Stop 4 weeks before surgery and use alternative
Stop 2 weeks after surgery to prevent infection
qs.e: The combined oral contraceptive pill should be stopped 4 weeks before major surgery to minimize the heightened risk of venous thromboembolism, and an alternative method of contraception should be provided. Stopping it on the morning of surgery is insufficient.

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: The combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) uses estrogen and progestogen to prevent ovulation, thicken cervical mucus and alter endometrium. It also regulates menstrual bleeding and treats acne. Clinicians must weigh benefits against thrombotic, hepatic and drug‑interaction risks.

sections.p: COCP is a daily oral medication containing synthetic estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) and a progestogen. Diagnosis is clinical: a woman who reports regular intake and has no contraindications.
b: No laboratory diagnosis required; history and physical confirm use and adherence

sections.p: Not applicable – COCP is a preventive therapy, not a disease with stages.

The pill’s mechanism is pharmacologic: estrogen stabilises the endometrium and progestogen suppresses the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑gonadal axis. Common contraindications include smoking >35 y, hypertension, migraine with aura, history of thromboembolism, liver disease, and pregnancy.
Patients present with regular menstrual cycles, reduced dysmenorrhoea, and sometimes acne improvement. Side effects may include nausea, breast tenderness, headache, and mood changes.
Investigations are reserved for contraindication screening.

t.b: Rule out anemia or thrombocytopenia; abnormal counts may indicate bleeding risk or underlying disease.
Assess hepatic function; abnormal values contraindicate estrogen use.
Confirm non‑pregnancy before initiation; positive test indicates need to discontinue.
Identify inherited clotting disorders; abnormal results may preclude COCP.

sections.p: Urgent complications include thromboembolism, stroke, myocardial infarction, hepatic adenoma, and severe hypertension. Red flags are sudden chest pain, dyspnea, severe headache, visual changes, or abdominal pain.
Management involves confirming eligibility, counseling on adherence and emergency contraception, and monitoring for adverse effects. If contraindications arise, switch to progestogen‑only methods.

t.b: Used when estrogen is contraindicated; reduces thrombotic risk.
Alternative for patients needing contraception without estrogen.

sections.p: Follow‑up at 3–6 months to assess bleeding pattern, side effects, and adherence. Prevention of complications includes lifestyle modification (smoking cessation, weight control) and regular BP checks.
COCP is often mistaken for progestogen‑only pill, which lacks estrogen and therefore does not increase thrombotic risk.
Normal liver enzymes may mask early hepatic dysfunction; normal BP may miss episodic hypertension. Pregnancy tests can be falsely negative if taken too early.

faq.q: Can COCP be used in a woman with migraine with aura?
faq.a: No, estrogen increases stroke risk in migraine with aura; use a progestogen‑only method instead.

faq.q: What should I do if I miss a dose?
faq.a: Take it as soon as remembered; if >12 h late, use backup contraception for 48 h.

faq.q: Does COCP affect fertility long term?
faq.a: No, fertility returns rapidly after discontinuation.
